THOUGHT: The patient has a solitary, slowly enlarging 2.5-cm, firm, mobile, painless subcutaneous nodule on the nape of the neck of 2 months' duration. The overlying skin cannot be pinched, suggesting the lesion is attached to the dermis (a common feature of epidermal inclusion/epidermoid cysts, which often have a central punctum and adherence to skin). Ultrasound shows a well-circumscribed, cystic subcutaneous lesion, which fits an epidermal inclusion cyst (typically well-defined with internal debris). There are no signs of infection (no pain, discharge, fever, normal WBC) and no regional lymphadenopathy. Although the patient has a history of colon cancer, cutaneous metastatic lesions from colon cancer are uncommon, generally present differently (may be multiple, firm, rapidly growing, sometimes ulcerated) and would be less likely to appear as a well-circumscribed superficial cyst on ultrasound. Other possibilities include a pilar (trichilemmal) cyst (more common on the scalp) or a benign lipoma (usually noncystic, softer), but the clinical and imaging features most strongly support an epidermal inclusion (epidermoid) cyst.

DIAGNOSIS: Epidermal inclusion (epidermoid) cyst of the posterior neck.
